options.C: Single-engine land and sea, multiengine land and sea.

text: To minimize the side loads placed on the landing gear during touchdown, the pilot should keep the

options.A: direction of motion of the aircraft parallel to the runway.
options.B: longitudinal axis of the aircraft parallel to the direction of its motion.
options.C: downwind wing lowered sufficiently to eliminate the tendency for the aircraft to drift.

explanation: Keeping the longitudinal axis parallel to the direction of motion ensures that the main gear will touchdown and roll as designed, parallel to the aircraft's direction of travel. Side loading the gear is not only bad for the aircraft structurally, but can result in the aircraft rolling away from the runway centerline on touchdown.

text: Where may an aircraft's operating limitations be found if the aircraft has an Experimental or Special light-sport airworthiness certificate?

options.B: In the current, FAA-approved flight manual.
options.C: In the aircraft airframe and engine logbooks

explanation: GFDPP 2-10, FAA Order 8130.2 Operating limitations for experimental aircraft are actually part of Form 8130-7, which is the special airworthiness certificate. As with all airworthiness certificates, this one must be carried in the aircraft, which ensures the operating limitations of an experimental or light sport aircraft are available to the PIC.

text: Excessively high engine temperatures will

options.A: cause damage to heat-conducting hoses and warping of the cylinder cooling fins.
options.B: cause loss of power, excessive oil consumption, and possible permanent internal engine damage.
options.C: not appreciably affect an aircraft engine.

explanation: High temperature can cause detonation and a resulting loss of power, excessive oil consumption, and engine damage, Including scoring of the cylinders and damage to pistons, rings, and valves.

text: If the engine oil temperature and cylinder head temperature gauges have exceeded their normal operating range, the pilot may have been operating with

options.C: too much power and with the mixture set too lean.

explanation: With high power settings and the mixture set too lean, overheating can result. This can be indicated by a high engine oil temperature and cylinder head temperature.

text: One purpose of the dual ignition system on an aircraft engine is to provide for
explanation: Dual ignition systems fire two spark plugs, which improves combustion of the fuel/air mixture and results in slightly more power.

text: On aircraft equipped with fuel pumps, when is the auxiliary electric driven pump used?

options.A: In the event engine-driven fuel pump fails.
options.B: All the time to aid the engine-driven fuel pump.
options.C: Constantly except in starting the engine.

explanation: The auxiliary electric pump is a backup for an enginedriven pump. Although labeling, procedures for use, and control switches differ between manufacturers, these auxiliary pumps can cause operational problems if used inappropriately. In some systems, continuous use of both the auxiliary pump and the engine-driven pump can cause an excessively rich mixture. Besides the back-up function, auxiliary pumps are commonly used to provide fuel under pressure for engine starting.

text: The operating principle of float-type carburetors is based on the

options.A: automatic metering of air at the venturi as the aircraft gains altitude.
options.B: difference in air pressure at the venturi throat and the air inlet.
options.C: increase in air velocity in the throat of a venturi.... causing an increase in air pressure.

explanation: The decreased pressure caused by air flowing rapidly through the venturi tube draws fuel from the float chamber.

text: The basic purpose of adjusting the fuel/air mixture at altitude is to

options.A: decrease the amount of fuel in the mixture in order to compensate for increased air density.
options.B: decrease the fuel flow in order to compensate for decreased air density.
options.C: increase the amount of fuel in the mixture to compensate for the decrease in pressure and density of the air.

explanation: If fuel flow is not decreased with altitude, the mixture becomes too rich with fuel. Therefore, the fuel mixture must be leaned to maintain the proper fuel/air ratio.

text: During the run-up at a high-elevation airport, a pilot notes a slight engine roughness that is not affected by the magneto check but grows worse during the carburetor heat check. Under these circumstances, what would be the most logical initial action?

options.A: Check the results obtained with a leaner setting of the mixture.
options.B: Taxi back to the flight line for a maintenance check.
options.C: Reduce manifold pressure to control detonation. The Powerplant and Related Systems.

explanation: In this case, engine roughness is probably caused by the mixture set too rich for the high altitude. When the carburetor heat is turned on, the warmer air entering the carburetor is less dense, and the mixture is further enriched. As a result, the engine roughness increases. The problem can usually be corrected by leaning the mixture.

text: While cruising at 9,500 feet MSL, the fuel/air mixture is properly adjusted. What will occur if a descent to 4,500 feet MSL is made without readjusting the mixture?

options.A: The fuel/air mixture may become excessively lean.
options.B: There will be more fuel in the cylinders than is needed for normal combustion, and the excess fuel will absorb heat and cool the engine.

text: Which condition is most favorable to the development of carburetor icing?

options.A: Any temperature below freezing and a relative humidity of less than 50 percent.
options.B: Temperature between 32° and 50°F and low humidity.
options.C: Temperature between 20° and 70°F and high humidity.

explanation: GFDPPM 2-19, PHB Carburetor icing is most likely between 20° and 70°F in high humidity conditions.

text: The possibility of carburetor icing exists even when the ambient air temperature is as

options.A: high as 70°F and the relative humidity is high.
options.B: high as 95°F and there is visible moisture.
options.C: low as 0°F and the relative humidity is high.

explanation: Carburetor icing is most probable between 20° and 70°F with high humidity or visible moisture.

text: If an aircraft is equipped with a fixed-pitch propeller and a float-type carburetor, the first indication of carburetor ice would most likely be

options.A: a drop in oil temperature and cylinder head temperature.

explanation: The restricted airflow through the carburetor causes an enriched mixture and loss of RPM.

explanation: 21, PHB When the carburetor heat is turned on, the warmer air entering the carburetor is less dense, and the mixture is enriched.

text: Generally speaking, the use of carburetor heat tends to

options.C: have no effect on engine performance.

explanation: Since the warmer air entering the carburetor Is less dense, the fuel/air mixture is enriched and power decreases.

text: The presence of carburetor ice in an aircraft equipped with a fixed-pitch propeller can be verified by applying carburetor heat and noting

options.A: an increase in RPM and then a gradual decrease in RPM.
options.B: a decrease in RPM and then a constant RPM indication.
options.C: a decrease in RPM and then a gradual increase in RPM.

explanation: When carburetor heat is first applied, the mixture is enriched, and RPM decreases. Then, as the ice melts, airflow into the carburetor increases, leaning the mixture, and RPM increases.

text: With regard to carburetor ice, float-type carburetor systems in comparison to fuel injection systems are generally considered to be

options.C: susceptible to icing only when visible moisture is present. The Powerp/ant and Related Systems.

explanation: Because fuel injection systems do not have a venturi throat, they are not as susceptible to icing as float-type carburetors.

text: If the grade of fuel used in an aircraft engine is lower than specified for the engine, it will most likely cause

options.A: a mixture of fuel and air that is not uniform in all cylinders.

explanation: The higher the grade of fuel, the more pressure it can withstand without detonating. Conversely, lower fuel grades are more prone to detonation.

text: Detonation occurs in a reciprocating aircraft engine when

options.A: the spark plugs are fouled or shorted out or the wiring is defective.
options.B: hot spots in the combustion chamber ignite the fuel/ air mixture in advance of normal ignition.
options.C: the unburned charge in the cylinders explodes instead of burning normally.

explanation: Detonation occurs when the fuel/air mixture suddenly explodes in the cylinders instead of burning smoothly.

text: Detonation may occur at high-power settings when

options.A: the fuel mixture ignites instantaneously instead of burning progressively and evenly.
options.B: an excessively rich fuel mixture causes an explosive gain in power.
options.C: the fuel mixture is ignited too early by hot carbon deposits in. the cylinder.

explanation: GFDPP-2-25, PHB Detonation occurs when the fuel/air mixture suddenly explodes in the cylinders instead of burning smoothly. Detonation is caused by excessively lean mixtures while hot spots in the cylinder describes pre-ignition.

text: If a pilot suspects that the engine (with a fixed-pitch propeller) is detonating during climb-out after takeoff, the initial corrective action to take would be to

options.B: lower the nose slightly to increase airspeed.

explanation: Detonation can occur when the engine overheats. One action to help cool the engine is to increase airspeed, thus increasing the cooling airflow around the engine.

explanation: Pre-ignition occurs when the fuel/air mixture ignites too soon.

options.A: Reduce rate of climb and increase airspeed.
options.B: Reduce climb speed and increase RPM.
options.C: Increase climb speed and increase RPM.

text: How is engine operation controlled on an engine equipped with a constant-speed propeller?

options.A: The throttle controls power output as registered on the manifold pressure gauge and the propeller control regulates engine RPM.
options.B: The throttle controls power output as registered on the manifold pressure gauge and the propeller control regulates a constant blade angle.
options.C: The throttle controls engine RPM as registered on the tachometer and the mixture control regulates the power output.

explanation: GFDPPM 2-38, PHB The throttle controls the power output of the engine, which is indicated on the manifold pressure gauge. The propeller control changes the pitch of the propeller blades, thus controlling engine RPM, which is indicated on the tachometer.

text: What is an advantage of a constant-speed propeller?

options.A: Permits the pilot to select and maintain a desired cruising speed.
options.B: Permits the pilot to select the blade angle for the most efficient perfonnance.
options.C: Provides a smoother operation with stable RPM and eliminates vibrations.

explanation: By selecting the proper blade angle, the pilot can convert a high percentage of engine power into thrust over a wide range of RPM and airspeed combinations. This allows the most efficient performance to be gained from the engine.

text: A precaution for the operation of an engine equipped with a constant-speed propeller is to

options.A: avoid high RPM settings with high manifold pressure.
options.B: avoid high manifold pressure settings with low RPM.
options.C: always use a rich mixture with high RPM settings.

explanation: For a given RPM setting; there is a maximum allowable manifold pressure. Generally, high manifold pressures with low RPM should be avoided to prevent internal stress within the engine.

text: What should be the first action after starting an aircraft engine?

options.A: Adjust for proper RPM and check for desired indications on the engine gauges.
options.B: Place the magneto or ignition switch momentarily in the OFF position to check for proper grounding.
options.C: Test each brake and the parking brake.

explanation: Immediately after starting an engine, set the proper RPM and check engine gauges for proper indications.

text: Should it become necessary to handprop an airplane engine, it is extremely important that a competent pilot

options.B: be at the controls in the cockpit.
options.C: be in the cockpit and call out all commands. The Powerplant and Related Systems.

explanation: When hand-propping an airplane, a competent pilot must be at the controls to prevent the airplane from moving and to set the engine controls properly.

text: Excessively high engine temperatures, either in the air or on the ground, will

options.A: increase fuel consumption and may increase power due to the increased heat.
options.B: result in damage to heat-conducting hoses and warping of cylinder cooling fans.
options.C: cause loss of power, excessive oil consumption, and possible permanent internal engine damage.

explanation: High temperatures can cause detonation and a resulting loss of power, excessive oil consumption, and engine damage, including scoring of the cylinders and damage to piston, rings, and valves.

text: To prope!lY purge water from the fuel system of an aircraft equipped with fuel tank sumps and a fuel strainer quick drain, it is necessary to drain fuel from the

options.B: lowest point in the fuel system.
options.C: fuel strainer drain and the fuel tank sumps

explanation: When the fuel strainer is being drained, water in the tank may not appear until all the fuel has been drained from the lines leading to the tank. Therefore, drain enough fuel from the fuel strainer to be certain that fuel is being drained from the tank. The amount will depend on the length of the fuel line from the tank to the drain. Water may also remain in the fuel tank even after the fuel strainer has ceased to show any trace of water. This residual water can be removed only by draining the fuel tank sump drains.

text: How do variations in temperature affect the altimeter?

options.A: Pressure levels are raised on warm days and the indicated altitude is lower than true altitude.
options.B: Higher temperatures expand the pressure levels and the indicated altitude is higher than true altitude.
options.C: Lower temperatures lower the pressure levels and the indicated altitude is lower than true altitude.

explanation: Because atmospheric pressure levels are raised on warm days, the aircraft will be at a higher altitude than indicated. In other words, the Indicated altitude is lower than true altitude.

text: What is true altitude?

options.A: The vertical distance of the aircraft above sea level.
options.B: The vertical distance of the aircraft above the surface.
options.C: The height above the standard daturn plane.

explanation: True altitude is the actual height (vertical distance) above mean sea level.

text: What is absolute altitude?

options.A: The altitude read directly from the altimeter.
options.B: The vertical distance of the aircraft above the surface.
options.C: The height above the standard daturn plane.

explanation: Absolute altitude is the height (vertical distance) above the surface.

text: What is density altitude?

options.A: The height above the standard daturn plane.
options.B: The pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature.
options.C: The altitude read directly from the altimeter.

explanation: Density altitude is found by applying a correction for nonstandard temperature to the pressure altitude.

text: What is pressure altitude?

options.A: The indicated altitude corrected for position and installation error.
options.B: The altitude indicated when the barometric pressure scale is set to 29.92.
options.C: The indicated altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature and pressure.

explanation: Pressure altitude is the height above the standard daturn plane when 29.92 is set in the scale.

options.C: emain the same regardless of altitude.

explanation: Since airspeed Indicators are calibrated to read true airspeed only under standard sea level conditions, the indicated airspeed does not reflect lower air density at higher altitudes. As a result, the indicated airspeed of a stall remains the same.

explanation: The red line is the never-exceed speed.

text: (Refer to figure 4.) What is the maximum structural cruising speed?

text: What is an important airspeed limitation that is not color coded on airspeed indicators?
explanation: The maneuvering speed of an airplane is not shown on the airspeed indicator. It can be found in the airplane manual or on placards.

options.A: movement of the aircraft about the yaw and roll axes.

text: When making routine transponder code changes, pilots should avoid inadvertent selection of which code?
explanation: You should avoid inadvertent selection of transponder codes which may set off false alarms at radar facilities. These codes are: 7500 for hijacking, 7600 for radio communications failure, and 7700 for emergencies.

text: When operating under VFR below 18,000 feet MSL, unless otherwise authorized, what transponder code should be selected?
explanation: The transponder code for VFR aircraft is 1200. Aircraft operating above 18,000 feet MSL are in Class A airspace and must have an IFR clearance.

text: Unless otherwise authorized, if flying a transponder equipped aircraft, a pilot should squawk which VFR code?
explanation: The transponder code for VFR aircraft is 1200. Aircraft operating above 18,000 feet MSL are in Class A airspace and must have an I FR clearance.

text: If Air Traffic Control advises that radar service is terminated when the pilot is departing Class C airspace, the transponder should be set to code
explanation: Since you would then be operating under VFR, the transponder should be set to 1200.

text: When an air traffic controller issues radar traffic information in relation to the 12-hour clock, the reference the controller uses is the aircraft's
explanation: Controllers can see an aircraft's ground track on radar, but cannot factor in any crab angle applied for wind correction. Pilots should consider this when reacting to ATC traffic advisories.

text: Absence of the sky condition and visibility on an Al11S broadcast indicates that

options.A: weather conditions are at or above VFR minimums.
options.B: the sky condition is clear and visibilnfy is unrestricted.
options.C: the ceiling is at least 5,000 feet and visibility is 5 miles or more.

explanation: If the ceiling is at least 5,000 feet and visibility is 5 miles or more, reporting of the ceiling/sky condition, visibility, and obstructions to vision is optional.

text: As Pilot in Command of an aircraft, under which situation can you deviate from an ATC clearance?

options.A: When operating in Class A airspace at night.
options.B: If an ATC clearance is not understood and in VFR conditions.
options.C: In response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory

explanation: Pilots who deviate for a resolution advisory must be responding to a TCAS II system. Those pilots must also report the deviation to ATC as soon as possible. Remember that there may be other reasons for deviating from and ATC clearance, since the PIC may deviate from any clearance if such action is necessary to ensure the safety of the flight.

text: A steady green light signal directed from the control tower to an aircraft in flight is a signal that the pilot

options.B: should give way to other aircraft and continue circling.

explanation: FAR 91.125 A steady green light while in flight means you are cleared to land.

text: Which light signal from the control tower clears a pilot to taxi?
explanation: FAR 91.125 While on the ground, a flashing green light means cleared to taxi.

text: If the control tower uses a light signal to direct a pilot to give way to other aircraft and continue circling, the light will be

options.C: alternating red and green. Radio Procedures.

explanation: FAR 91.125 While in flight, a steady red light means give way and '. continue circling.

text: A flashing white light signal from the control tower to a taxiing aircraft is an indication to

options.B: taxi only on taxiways and not cross runways.
options.C: return to the starting point on the airport.

explanation: FAR 91.125 A flashing white light while operating on the ground means return to the starting point on the airport.

text: An alternating red and green light signal directed from the control tower to an aircraft in flight is a signal to

options.C: not land; the airport is unsafe.

explanation: FAR 91.125 An alternating red and green signal means the same whether you are in flight or on the ground - exercise extreme caution.

text: While on final approach for landing, an alternating green and red light followed by a flashing red light is received from the control tower. Under these circumstances, the pilot should

options.A: discontinue the approach, fly the same traffic pattern and approach again, and land.
options.B: exercise extreme caution and abandon the approach, realizing the airport is unsafe for landing.
options.C: abandon the approach, circle the airport to the right, and expect a flashing white light when the airport is safe for landing.

explanation: FAR 91.125 An alternating red and green signal means exercise extreme caution. This is followed by a flashing red signal, which, in flight, means that the airport is unsafe.

text: (Refer to figure 28.) An aircraft departs an airport in the eastern daylight time zone at 0945 EDT for a 2-hour flight to an airport located in the central daylight time zone. The landing should be at what coord.inated universal time?
explanation: To convert the local departure time to UTC, add 4 hours (0945 + 4:00 = 1345). Two hours later is 15452.

text: (Refer to figure 28.) An aircraft departs an airport in the central standard time zone at Ov930 CST for a 2-hour flight to an airport located in the mountain standard time zone. The landing should be at what time?
explanation: Add 2 hours to the 0930 departure time to find the arrival time of 1130 CST. Since Mountain time is 1 hour earlier than Central, subtract 1 hour, for a landing time of 1030 MST.

text: (Refer to figure 28.) An aircraft departs an airport in the central standard time zone at 0845 CST for a 2-hour flight to an airport located in the mountain standard time zone. The landing should be at what coordinated universal time?
explanation: Departure time (0845) plus 2 hours is 1045 CST. Convert CST to UTC by adding 6 hours, for a landing time of 16452.

text: (Refer to figure 28.) An aircraft departs an airport in the mountain standard time zone at 1615 MST for a 2-hour 15-minute flight to an airport located in the Pacific standard time zone. The estimated time of arrival at the destination airport should be
explanation: Add 2:15 to 1615 MST to find the arrival time of 1830 MST. Since Pacific time is one hour earlier than MST, the arrival time is 1730 PST.

text: (Refer to figure 28.) An aircraft departs an airport in the Pacific standard time zone at 1030 PST for a 4-hour flight to an airport located in the central standard time zone. The landing should be at what coordinated universal time?
explanation: Add 4 hours to 1030 PST to find the arrival time of 1430 PST. To convert PST to UTC, add 8 hours. The landing time is 22302.

text: (Refer to figure 28.) An aircraft departs an airport in the mountain standard time zone at 1515 MST for a 2-hour 30-minute flight to an airport located in the Pacific standard time zone. What is the estimated time of arrival at the destination airport?
explanation: Add 2:30 to 1515 MST to find the arrival time of 1745 MST. Convert MST to PST by subtracting 1 hour. The answer is 1645 PST.

text: If the aircraft's radio fails, what is the recommended procedure when landing at a controlled airport?

options.A: Observe the traffic flow, enter the pattern, and look for a light signal from the tower.
options.B: Enter a crosswind leg and rock the wings.
options.C: Flash the landing lights and cycle the landing gear while circling the airport.

explanation: To avoid conflicts and cause the least disruption in the traffic flow, determine the landing direction, and enter the pattern. Watch the tower for a light signal and acknowledge by rocking the wings. At night, acknowledge by flashing the landing or navigation lights.

text: After landing at a tower-controlled airport, when should the pilot contact ground control?

options.A: When advised by the tower to do so.
options.B: Prior to turning off the runway.
options.C: After reaching a taxiway that leads directly to the parking area. Radio Procedures.

explanation: The tower will normally instruct you to exit the runway and contact ground control.

text: If instructed by ground control to taxi to Runway 9, the pilot may proceed

options.B: to the next intersecting runway where further clearance is required.
options.C: via taxiways and across runways to Runway 9, where an immediate takeoff may be made.

explanation: A clearance to taxi to a runway allows the pilot to proceed to that runway and cross any intersecting runways.

options.B: At 15 and 45 minutes past the hour.

text: What causes variations in altimeter settings between weather reporting points?

options.A: Unequal heating of the Earth's surface.

explanation: AW Temperature changes cause variations in air pressure and density. Because the earth's surface is heated unevenly, altimeter settings will be different between weather stations.

text: The wind at 5,000 feet AGL is southwesterly while the surface wind is southerly. This difference in direction is primarily due to

options.A: stronger pressure gradient at higher altitudes.
options.B: friction between the wind and the surface.
options.C: stronger Coriolis force at the surface.

explanation: AW Above 2,000 feet AGL, wind flows along isobars. Below that altitude, friction with the earth's surface deflects the wind.

text: Convective circulation patterns associated with sea breezes are caused by

options.A: warm, dense air moving inland from over the water.
options.B: water absorbing and radiating heat faster than the land.
options.C: cool, dense air moving inland from over the water. Weather Patterns

explanation: AW During the day, land surfaces become warmer than the adjacent water surfaces. This warms the air above the land causing the air to rise. The rising air is replaced by the inland flow of cooler, denser air located over the water. As the warm air flows over the water it cools and descends. This starts the cycle all over again. During the night, the process is reversed as the land cools off faster than the water.

text: How will frost on the wings of an airplane affect takeoff performance?

options.A: Frost will disrupt the smooth flow of air over the wing, adversely affecting its lifting capability.
options.B: Frost will change the camber of the wing, increasing its lifting capability.
options.C: Frost will cause the airplane to become airborne with a 11igher angle of attack, decreasing the stall speed.

explanation: Frost disrupts the smooth airflow over the wing and can cause early separation of the airflow, resulting in a loss of lift.

text: Every pbysical process of weather is accompanied by, or is the result of, a
explanation: AW Every physical process of weather such as heating, cooling, evaporation, and condensation, is caused by, or is the result of, a heat exchange.

text: A temperature inversion would most likely result in which weather condition?

options.A: Clouds with extensive vertical development above an inversion aloft.
options.B: Good visibility in the lower levels of the atmosphere and poor visibility above an inversion aloft.
options.C: An increase in temperature as altitude is increased.

explanation: AW Normally, temperature decreases with altitude. During an inversion, cooler air is trapped beneath a warmer layer of air. Therefore, temperature increases with altitude.

text: The most frequent type of ground or surface-based temperature inversion is that which is produced by

options.A: terrestrial radiation on a clear, relatively still night.
options.B: warm air being lifted rapidly aloft in the vicinity of mountamous terrain.
options.C: the movement of colder air under warm air, or the movement of warm air over cold air.

explanation: AW An inversion commonly forms on clear, cool nights when the ground radiates heat and cools faster than the overlying air.

text: Which weather conditions should be expected beneath a low-level temperature inversion layer when the relative humidity is high?

options.A: Smooth air, poor visibility, fog, haze, or low clouds.
options.B: Light wind shear, poor visibility, haze, and light ram.
options.C: Turbulent air, poor visibility, fog, low stratus type clouds, and showery precipitation.

explanation: AW Low-level temperature inversions normally occur in stable, smooth air, with poor visibility due to trapped pollutants which are commonly referred to as condensation nuclei. In addition, high humidity tends to cause formation of fog and low clouds.

text: What is meant by the tenn "dewpoint"?

options.A: The temperature at which condensation and evaporation are equal.
options.B: The temperature at which dew will always form.
options.C: The temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated.

explanation: AW When air is cooled to its dewpoint, it can hold no more moisture, and is said to be saturated.

text: The amount of water vapor which air can hold depends on the
explanation: AW The amount of moisture in the air primarily depends on the temperature. For example, warm air can hold more moisture than cool air.

text: Clouds, fog, or dew will always form when
explanation: AW Condensation occurs when water vapor changes to liquid form. Examples are when water vapor changes to clouds, fog, or dew.

text: Which conditions result in the formation of frost?

options.A: The temperature of the collecting surface is at or below freezing when small droplets of moisture fall on the surface.
options.B: The temperature of the collecting surface is at or below the dewpoint of the adjacent air and the dewpoint is below freezing.
options.C: The temperature of the surrounding air is at or below freezing when small drops of moisture fall on the collecting surface.

explanation: AW When the dewpoint of the surrounding air is below freezing, and the collecting surface is at or below the dewpoint, water vapor sublimates directly into ice crystals or frost instead of condensing into dew..

text: The presence of ice pellets at the surface is evidence that there

options.C: is a temperature inversion with freezing rain at a higher altitude.

explanation: AW Due to a temperature inversion, a warm layer of air is aloft and keeps the rain In liquid form. As the rain falls through colder air, it begins to freeze, finally turning into ice pellets. Ice pellets always Indicate freezing rain at a higher altitude. Ice pellets can form under various conditions, and do not necessarily indicate thunderstorms.

text: What measurement can be used to determine the stability of the atmosphere?
explanation: AW The stability of air refers to its resistance to displacement upward or downward; it is determined by the actual lapse rate. Lapse rate generally refers to the decrease in temperature with an increase in altitude. A high lapse rate tends to indicate unstable air, and a low lapse rate is an indicator of stability in the atmosphere.

text: What would decrease the stability of an air mass?
explanation: AW Stability is altered by a change in the lapse rate of an air mass. Warming from below or cooling from above will increase the lapse rate and make the air less stable.

text: What is a characteristic of stable air?
explanation: AW There Is very little vertical development of clouds In stable air, and stratiform clouds and poor visibility are typical. Cumulus clouds and good Visibility are indicators of unstable air..

text: Moist, stable air flowing upslope can be expected to
explanation: AW Stratus clouds are produced in stable air. When moist air flows upslope it cools to its saturation point, and clouds are formed.

text: If an unstable air mass is forced upward, what type clouds can be expected?
explanation: AW Clouds with extensive vertical development are formed when unstable air is lifted. These cumulus type clouds are associated with moderate to severe turbulence.

text: What feature is associated with a temperature inversion?
explanation: GFDPPM 6-17, AW Temperature inversions occur in stable air. Inversions cannot form in unstable air. As Chinook winds descend, the temperature rises. This is the opposite of an inversion (cooler air under a warmer layer). In the U.S., the typical example of Chinook winds is the downslope, easterly flow from the Rocky Mountains. 6-21 PLT512 What is the approximate base of the cumulus clouds if the surface air temperature at 1,000 feet MSL is 70°F and the dewpoint is 48°F? text: What is the approximate base of the cumulus clouds if the surface air temperature at 1,000 feet MSL is 70°F and the dewpoint is 48°F?
explanation: AW Cloud bases can be estimated by using a lapse rate of 4.5°F per 1,000 feet and the temperature/dewpoint spread (70 - 48 = 22). Divide 22 by 4.5 to find the approximate cloud base in thousands of feet. In this case, the cloud bases will be 4,889 (22 + 4.5 x 1,000) feet above the surface, or rounded to 5,000 feet. Since the surface is 1,000 feet MSL, the cloud base should be approximately 6,000 feet MSL.

text: At approximately what altitude above the surface would the pilot expect the base of cumuli form clouds if the surface air temperature is 82°F and the dewpoint is 38°F?
explanation: AW Cloud bases can be estimated by using a lapse rate of 4.5°F per 1,000 feet and the temperature/dewpoint spread.

text: What are characteristics of a moist, unstable air mass?
explanation: AW Cumuliform clouds are indicative of unstable air. These clouds normally produce showery, not continuous, precipitation. Poor visibility, smooth air, and stratiform clouds are characteristic of stable air.

text: What are characteristics of unstable air?

options.C: Nimbostratus clouds and good surface visibility.

explanation: AW The lifting motion of unstable air produces turbulence. Clouds and pollutants are not trapped as they are in stable layers of air, and good visibility is typical with unstable air. Poor surface visibility and nimbostratus clouds are typical of stable air masses.

text: A stable air mass is most likely to have which characteristic?
explanation: AW Stable air resists the lifting motion that is associated with turbulence, and is typically smooth. Showery precipitation and turbulent air are characteristics of unstable air.

text: The suffix "nimbus," used in naming clouds, means

options.A: a cloud with extensive vertical development.
options.C: a middle cloud containing ice pellets.

explanation: AW The word "nimbus" is the Latin word for rainstorm or cloud, and is used today to designate rain clouds, such as cumulonimbus or nimbostratus.

text: Clouds are divided into four families according to their
explanation: AW Clouds are also grouped by families according to their altitudes (height range). The four families are low, middle, high, and clouds with extensive vertical development.

text: The boundary between two different air masses is referred to as a
explanation: AW The boundary area where two air masses of different properties meet is called a front.

text: One of the most easily recognized discontinuities across a front is
explanation: AW Since a front is the boundary between air masses of differing temperatures, one of the easiest ways to recognize frontal passage is the change in temperature.

text: One weather phenomenon which will always occur when flying across a front is a change in the
explanation: AW A shift in wind direction always occurs across a front.

text: Steady precipitation preceding a front is an indication of

options.B: cumuliform clouds with little or no turbulence.
options.C: stratifonn clouds with little or no turbulence.

explanation: 32, AW Steady precipitation, stratiform clouds, and little or no turbulence are all typical of stable air.

text: What situation is most conducive to the formation of radiation fog?

options.A: Warm, moist air over low, flatland areas on clear, calm nights.
options.B: Moist, tropical air moving over cold, offshore water.
options.C: The movement of cold air over much warmer water.

explanation: AW On clear, calm nights in flat areas, radiation fog forms when moist air cools to its dewpoint. Ground fog is a form of radiation fog.

text: If the temperature/dewpoint spread is small and decreasing, and the temperature is 62°F, what type weather is most likely to develop?

options.C: Fog or low clouds. Weather Patterns.

explanation: AW When the temperature/dewpoint spread decreases to zero, the likely result is the condensation of water vapor into visible moisture, such as fog or low clouds.

text: In which situation is advection fog most likely to form?

options.A: A warm, moist air mass on the windward side of mountains.
options.B: An air mass moving inland from the coast in winter.
options.C: A ljght breeze blowing colder air out to sea.

explanation: AW On clear, calm nights in flat areas, radiation fog forms when moist air cools to its dewpoint. Ground fog is a form of radiation fog. When warmer air moves inland, advectlon fog is likely to form.

text: What types of fog depend upon wind in order to exist?.
explanation: AW On clear, calm nights in flat areas, radiation fog forms when moist air cools to its dewpoint. Ground fog is a form of radiation fog. When warmer air moves inland, advection fog is likely to form.

text: Low-level turbulence can occur and icing can become hazardous in which type of fog?
explanation: GFDPPM 6-23, AW Steam fog is formed by cold, dry air moving over warmer water. As the water particles evaporate and rise, they often freeze and fall back into the water. This section covers such hazards as thunderstorms, turbulence, icing and restrictions to visibility, addressing cause, as well as hazardous effects. THUNDERSTORMS • Cumulonimbus clouds have the greatest turbulence. • The conditions necessary for the formation of cumulonimbus clouds are a lifting action and unstable, moist air. • Thunderstorms are formed when high humidity, lifting force and unstable conditions combine. TYPES • Thunderstorms which generally produce the most intense hazard to aircraft are squall line thunderstorms. • A non-frontal, narrow band of active thunderstorms that often develops ahead of a cold front is known as a squall line. LIFE CYCLE • The cumulus stage of a thunderstorm is associated with a continuous updraft. • The mature stage of a thunderstorm begins with precipitation beginning to fall. • Thunderstorms reach their greatest intensity during the mature stage. • The dissipating stage is characterized predominantly by downdrafts. text: What is the most effective way to use the eyes during night flight? -

options.A: Look only at far away, dim lights.
options.B: Scan slowly to permit off center viewing.
options.C: Concentrate directly on each object for a few seconds.

explanation: The rods in the retina are used for night vision. Because they are not located directly behind the pupil, you must use off center viewing. Also, in dim light, you might need to move your eyes more slowly to prevent blurring of images than during the day.

text: The best method to use when looking for other traffic at night is to

options.A: look to the side of the object and scan slowly.
options.B: scan the visual field very rapidly.
options.C: look to the side of the object and scan rapidly.

explanation: The most effective method of night scanning is to use off center vision, which means looking to the side of an object, and to scan slowly to prevent blurring.

text: The most effective method of scanning for other aircraft for collision avoidance during nighttime hours is to use

options.A: regularly spaced concentration on the 3-, 9-, and 12-o' clock positions.
options.B: a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements to search each 30-degree sector.
options.C: peripheral vision by scanning small sectors and utilizing off center viewing.

explanation: FTH As with the previous questions, scanning should be done slowly, in small sectors, using offcenter (peripheral) vision.

text: During a night flight, you observe a steady red light and a flashing red light ahead and at the same altitude. What is the general direction of movement of the other aircraft?

options.A: The other aircraft is flying away from you.
options.B: The other aircraft is crossing to the left.
options.C: The other aircraft is crossing to the right.

explanation: ; AFH The steady red light is a position light on the left wing and the flashing red light is an anticollision beacon. If you are looking at the left wingtip, the other aircraft would be crossing to the left.

text: During a night flight, you observe a steady white light and a flashing red light ahead and at the same altitude. What is the general direction of movement of the other aircraft?

options.A: The other aircraft is flying away from you.
options.B: The other aircraft is crossing to the left.
options.C: The other aircraft is crossing to the right.

explanation: GFDPPM 10-5, AFH The white position light is on the tail and the flashing red light is the anticollision light. Therefore, you would be looking at the rear of the aircraft, which indicates it is flying away from you.

text: During a night flight, you observe steady red and green lights ahead and at the same altitude. What is the general direction of movement of the other aircraft?

options.A: The other aircraft is crossing to the Jeft.
options.B: The other aircraft is flying away from you.
options.C: The other aircraft is approaching head-on.

explanation: In this case, you are seeing both wingtip lights. If there was no white tail light in between them, you would most likely be looking head-on at the aircraft.

explanation: You should try to make night VFR approaches the same as day approaches.

text: When a stressful situation is encountered in flight, an abnormal increase in the volume of air breathed in and out can cause a condition known as
explanation: GFDPPM 10-18, AIM Hyperventilation occurs when the breathing rate is too rapid or too deep. It usually occurs with stress and can occur with or without the use of supplemental oxygen. Aerosinusitis is an inflammation of the sinuses and aerotitis is an inflammation of the middle ear. Both are caused by changes in air pressure.

text: Which would most likely result in hyperventilation?

options.C: An extremely slow rate ofbreathing and insu.fficient oxygen.

explanation: Emotional tension, anxiety, and fear can cause the rapid, deep breathing associated with hyperventilation.

text: A pilot experiencing the effects of hyperventilation should be able to restore the proper carbon dioxide level in the body by

options.A: slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a paper bag, or talking al.oud.
options.B: breathing spontaneously and deeply or gaining mental control of the situation.
options.C: increasing the breathing rate in order to increase lung ventilation.

explanation: Slowing the breathing rate is one of the best ways to stop hyperventilation. Breathing into a bag and talking aloud are also helpful.

explanation: 15, AC 20-32 Since carbon monoxide poisoning is a form of hypoxia, its effects are increased with altitude, where there is less oxygen available.

text: What preparation should a pilot make to adapt the eyes for night flying?

options.A: Wear sunglasses after sunset until ready for flight.
options.B: Avoid red lights at least 30 minutes before the flight.
options.C: Avoid bright white lights at least 30 minutes before the flight.

explanation: The rods In the human eye can take up to 30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark. Bright lights must be avoided for this amount of time.

text: The danger of spatial disorientation during flight in poor visual conditions may be reduced by

options.A: shifting the eyes quickly between the exterior visual field and the instrument panel.
options.B: having faith in the instruments rather than taking a chance on the sensory organs.
options.C: leaning the body in the opposite direction of the motion of the aircraft.

explanation: To avoid spatial disorientation, a pilot must rely on the Instruments in the cockpit and not the feelings from the sensory organs.

text: A lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude, or movement of the aircraft in space is defined as
explanation: Spatial disorientation occurs when visual cues are removed and the vestibular system in the inner ear and the somatosensory system (nerves and hearing) provide conflicting information to the brain.

text: Pilots are more subject to spatial disorientation if

options.A: they ignore the sensations of Euscles and inner ear.
options.B: visual cues are taken away, as they are in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC).
options.C: eyes are moved often in the process of cross-checking the flight instruments.

explanation: During flight in visual meteorological conditions (VMC), the eyes are the major orientation source and usually prevail over false sensations from other sensory systems. When these visual cues are taken away, as they are in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), false sensations can cause a pilot to quickly become disoriented. Pilots can overcome spatial disorientation if they ignore the sensations of muscles and innerear and focus on the flight instruments. Moving the eyes often to cross-check the flight instruments is a proper scanning technique that helps prevent spatial disorientation.

text: If a pilot experiences spatial disorientation during flight in a restricted visibility condition, the best way to overcome the effect is to

options.A: rely upon the aircraft instrument indications.
options.B: concentrate on yaw, pitch, and roll sensations.
options.C: consciously slow the breathing rate until symptoms clear and then resume normal breathing rate

explanation: Since the brain receives confusing messages from the body's senses, the pilot must rely on the aircraft's instruments.

text: What is it often called when a pilot pushes his or her capabilities and the aircraft's limits by trying to maintain visual contact with the terrain in low visibility and ceiling?
explanation: AC 60-22 Scud running is one of the operational pitfalls, describing a pilot that tries to maintain visual contact with the surface in low visibility and ceiling. Mind set is another operational pitfall that describes the inability to recognize and cope with changes in the situation different f rem those anticipated or planned. Peer pressure is an operational pitfall that describes poor decision making based upon emotional response to peers, rather than evaluating a situation objectively.

text: What is the antidote when a pilot has a hazardous attitude, such as "Antiauthority"?

options.A: Rules do not apply in this situation.
options.B: I know what I am doing.

explanation: AC 60-22 The antidote for the hazardous attitude, "Antiauthority" is: Follow the rules, they are usually right. "Rules do not apply in this situation" and "I know what I am doing" are not antidotes to any of the hazardous attitudes.

text: What antidotal phrase can help reverse the hazardous attitude of impulsivity?

options.B: Do it quickly to get it over with.

explanation: AC 60-22 The antidote for the hazardous attitude, "lmpulsivity" is: Not so fast, think first. "It could happen to me" and "Do it quickly to get it over with" are not antidotes to any of the hazardous attitudes.

text: What is the antidote when a pilot has a hazardous attitudet such as "Invulnerability"?

options.A: It will not happen to me.

explanation: AC 60-22 The antidote for the hazardous attitude, "Invulnerability" is: It could happen to me. "It will not happen to me'' and "It can not be that bad" are not antidotes to any of the hazardous attitudes..

text: What is the antidote when a pilot has a hazardous attitude, such as "Macho"?
explanation: AC 60-22 The antidote for the hazardous attitude, "Macho" is: Taking chances is foolish. "I can do it" and "Nothing will happen" are not antidotes to any of the hazardous attitudes.

text: What is the antidote when a pilot bas a hazardous attitude, such as "Resignation"?
explanation: AC 60-22 The antidote for the hazardous attitude, "Resignation" is: I am not helpless. "What is the use" and "Someone else is responsible'' are not antidotes to any of the hazardous attitudes.

text: Who is responsible for determining whether a pilot is fit to fly for a particular flight, even though he or she holds a current medical certificate?
explanation: AC 60-22 You, the pilot, are always responsible for determining if you are fit to fly for a particular flight. The FAA and medical examiners determine if you are fit to hold a medical certificate.

text: What is the one common factor which affects most preventable accidents?
explanation: AC 60-22 Most preventable accidents have one common factor: human error rather than a mechanical malfunction or structural failure. According to NTSB statistics gathered from 1992 to 1996, the pilot was the general cause or a contributing factor in 49% of the accidents. Whereas the aircraft only accounted for 19% of the accidents.

text: What often leads to spatial disorientation or collision with ground/obstacles when flying under Visual Flight Rules (VFR)?
explanation: AC 60-22 Continuing flight under VFR into instrument conditions often leads to spatial disorientation or collision with ground/obstacles. Getting behind the aircraft does not normally result in spatial disorientation or collision with the ground. Although duck-under syndrome often leads to impact with the ground, it normally does not result in spatial disorientatio

text: Hazardous attitudes occur to every pilot to some degree at some time. What are some of these hazardous attitudes? -

options.A: Poor risk management and lack of stress management.
options.B: Antiauthority, impulsivity, macho, resignation, and invulnerability.
options.C: Poor, snap judgments, and lack of a decision making process.

explanation: The commonly listed hazardous attitudes are antiauthority, impulsivity, macho, resignation, and invulnerability. Section D - NTSB 830—Aircraft Accident and Incident Reporting 12-35 SECTION D - NTSB 830—AIRCRAFT ACCIDENT AND INCIDENT REPORTING Pilots need to be familiar with the procedures and requirements for reporting aircraft accidents, incidents and overdue aircraft to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB). ACCIDENTS • If an aircraft is involved in an accident which results in substantial damage to the aircraft, the nearest NTSB field office should be notified immediately. • Aircraft wreckage may be moved prior to the time the NTSB takes custody, but only to protect the wreckage from further damage. • The owner of an aircraft that has been involved in an accident is required to file an accident report within 10 days. INCIDENTS • A flight control system malfunction or failure, and an in flight fire are two incidents that require immediate notification to the nearest NTSB field office. • An overdue aircraft that is believed to be involved in an accident must be immediately reported to the nearest NTSB field office. • The operator of an aircraft that has been involved in an incident is required to submit a report to the nearest NTSB field office when requested. 12-124 PLT366 If an aircraft is involved in an accident which results in substantial damage to the aircraft, the nearest NTSB field office should be notified A -immediately.
